candidate.answerReason: With 200 students per group, the exact probability is (199 × 198)/(599 × 598), approximately 0.1100, which is closest to 1/9.

methods.label: Count pairs of seats
methods.explanation:
Each lunch group contains \(600\div3=200\) students. Model the assignment by randomly filling \(600\) distinct seats, with \(200\) seats belonging to each lunch group. This keeps every group at its required size.

Whichever seat Al takes, \(599\) seats remain for Bob. After Bob takes a seat, \(598\) remain for Carol. Thus there are \(599\cdot598\) equally likely ordered pairs of seats for Bob and Carol. Each pair is counted once because Bob's seat is specified first and Carol's second.

For all three friends to share Al's group, Bob must take one of its \(199\) remaining seats. Carol must then take one of the \(198\) seats still available in that group. These \(199\cdot198\) pairs are exactly the favorable pairs. The counts are the same wherever Al sits, so the probability is
\[
\frac{199\cdot198}{599\cdot598}
=\frac{39{,}402}{358{,}202}
\approx0.1100.
\]
Since \(\frac19\approx0.1111\), the closest listed approximation is \(\frac19\), choice B.
methods.levelReason: The solution counts two successive seat choices and divides favorable outcomes by equally likely outcomes. It needs no combination formulas or formal conditional probability.

The method respects the fixed group sizes without assuming independence. These annotations describe the mathematics used, not student mastery.
